PAPER: Corpus Pragmatics (2026) 10:14 https://doi.org/10.1007/s41701-025-00214-4 RESEARCH Subtitling Arabic Cultural References into English: The Case of Brando El Sharq Amin Alquran1 · Ali Almanna1 · Amer Al-Adwan1 Received: 25 August 2025 / Accepted: 2 November 2025 © The Author(s) 2025 Abstract This study investigates the intricacies of subtitling cultural references (CRs) from the Lebanese Arabic dialect into English. Focusing on the ten-episode Lebanese Ar- abic series Brando El Sharq (Amin Dora, 2023), the study examines the challenges faced by subtitlers when dealing with cultural references, delving into the subti- tling decisions and strategies employed to render CRs from Arabic into English. The methodology for this descriptive study involves the collection, examination, and interpretation of data within the context of relevant academic literature. Pri- marily relying on Pedersen's (2005) strategies: Direct Translation, Generalization, Retention, Substitution, Specification, official equivalence, and Omission, the study analyzes the subtitler’s challenges and the approaches utilized to address them. Following a comprehensive analysis of these strategies, this study identifies the predominant and most popular strategies employed to subtitle CRs from Arabic to English. It also assesses whether Pedersen’s (2005) model provides sufficient strate- gies for rendering the CRs in Brando El Sharq (2023) and identifies any additional strategies utilized in subtitling the series. Moreover, the study reveals instances of mistranslation within the series, suggesting potential corrections and alternative ap- proaches to effectively convey CRs. Alquran et al. Introduction Since antiquity, the process of translating languages exchanged between nations across the globe has remained relatively consistent. However, the remarkable techno- logical advancements witnessed in contemporary times have the potential to mark a turning point, transcending the traditional linguistic scope of subtitling and ushering in a new era of cultural connectivity on a scale unprecedented in the past. In the realm of global communication and entertainment, Audiovisual Translation has emerged as an indispensable tool, enabling individuals from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds to access and appreciate a wide range of media. Yet, the translation of cultural references presents a formidable challenge for subtitlers, who must delicately balance linguistic and cultural specificity with the imperative to avoid causing offense, discomfort, or a loss of meaning for viewers. Each language carries its own unique cultural references. The concepts of cultural and linguistic relativity gained prominence in the United States during the 1970s. This anthropological inquiry gave rise to the postmodern- ist perspective, which posits that while cross-cultural understanding is a laudable goal, all cultures are inherently distinct and different. Translating one culture into another, particularly into a Western language, is a challenging, if not impossible, endeavor. Conversely, some scholars advocate for the existence of universals in lan- guage and culture. These universals are fundamental commonalities that transcend seemingly diverse languages and cultures. For instance, the concept of greetings is a universal phenomenon. Every culture possesses its own means of acknowledging and interacting with others upon meeting. Adherents of this perspective believe that these universals enable us to identify patterns and make generalizations. By applying these generalizations, foreign texts, such as an ancient poem about friendship, can be viewed as somewhat predictable. We can anticipate themes of loyalty, trust, and shared experiences, even if expressed through different cultural lenses. In this sense, foreign texts are not entirely alien but rather variations on familiar themes, akin to diverse cultural interpretations of the universal concept of friendship (Rosman & Rubel, 2003). Cultural references (CRs) are intrinsically tied to the unique characteristics of each language, reflecting the distinctive essence of its respective culture. While subtitling cultural references is essential for fostering cross-national communication, it presents a formidable challenge for subtitlers due to the constraints imposed upon them. One of the most significant obstacles encountered by subtitlers when translating CRs from the Source Culture (SC) lies in finding suitable equivalents within the Target Culture (TC). Given the linguistic and cultural disparities between Arabic and English, subti- tling Arabic cultural references into English demands considerable time and effort. Arabic’s extensive vocabulary, complex syntactic structures, and rich tapestry of cultural idioms and expressions attest to its profound cultural heritage (Al-Khalifa, 2002). Subtitlers must carefully navigate language equivalency, cultural sensitivity, and audience comprehension when translating these cultural references into English (Abu-Hamdieh, 2013). One of the primary challenges lies in identifying appropriate English translations for Arabic cultural references. 1 3 Subtitling Arabic Cultural References into English: The Case of Brando… Page 3 of 26 14 Arabic is replete with idioms and metaphors that pose significant obstacles for subtitlers translating into English, making it challenging to convey the complete meaning and cultural context. Subtitlers may need to modify or clarify specific refer- ences to ensure that the intended meaning is comprehensible to the target audience (Al-Adwan & Thawabteh, 2021). In recent years, the Arab world has transitioned from a passive recipient of trans- lated cinematic and television works to an active exporter of its own productions. Numerous Arabic works have been dubbed and subtitled into international lan- guages, most notably English. Prominent examples include “The Message” (1976), a biographical film about the life of Prophet Muhammad, “Omniscient” (2020), an Egyptian mystery thriller series, and “Jinn” (2019), a Jordanian supernatural teen drama series infused with elements of folklore and mythology. In 2010, the Egyptian series “Critical Moments” demonstrated innovation in two key spheres: technical and marketing. From a technical perspective, the series pio- neered the concept of Multiple Language Production, with the entirety of its second season translated into English, Chinese, and Persian. In terms of marketing, “Critical Moments” exhibited innovation by strategically targeting an International Audience and leveraging New Media Platforms. (IMDB, 2024). In light of what has been men- tioned earlier, this study aims to answer the following three questions: 1. What are the most commonly used strategies for translating Arabic cultural refer- ences in Brando El Sharq into English? 2. Has the subtitler conveyed the cultural references accurately? If not, what kinds of semantic or cultural losses can be observed? 3. To what extent have the strategies employed influenced the storyline of the series and the representation of the characters? Literature Review This section delves into the intricate domain of audiovisual translation, with a par- ticular focus on the nuanced art of subtitling. We shall investigate the multifaceted nature of culture and its profound influence on audiovisual material. A thorough understanding of cultural references is indispensable for proficient subtitling, as it serves to bridge the communicative gap between the source material and audiences hailing from diverse cultural backgrounds (Ivarsson, 1992). Subtitling, a specialized branch of translation, is uniquely intertwined with audio- visual content. It entails the meticulous translation of spoken and written dialogue, as well as other auditory elements, into written text. This textual rendition is strategi- cally positioned at the bottom of the screen, ensuring synchronization with the cor- responding audio content. As stated by Diaz-Cintas & Remael (2007, p. 8), subtitling refers to “the transla- tion practice of presenting a written text, usually on the lower part of the screen, that 1 3 14 Page 4 of 26 A. Alquran et al. conforms to the original dialogue of the speakers, in addition to the discursive com- ponents that appear on the screen and any information appearing on the soundtrack.” Gottlieb (2001, p.87) defines subtitling as “the rendering in a different language of verbal messages in film media, in the shape of one or more lines of written text presented on the screen in sync with the original written message.” Based on these definitions, subtitlers have to abide by spatial and temporal constraints of the medium which bear a significant role in achieving the final message of the translation appear- ing on the screen. Malenova (2015) classifies cultural references (e.g. ethical terms, religious terms) as social restrictions in the process of subtitling that include lexical items and expres- sions related to culture. Notwithstanding the foregoing, several constraints impede the subtitling process. These constraints can be categorized into normative, social, personal, and physi- ological restrictions. Normative restrictions arise from the challenge of identifying suitable equivalents for source text words within the target text. Social restrictions encompass lexical items and expressions deeply rooted in cultural context, such as religious and ethical terms. Subtitling is subject to various guidelines that address the technical spatial and temporal constraints inherent to the medium. These technical limitations exert a sig- nificant influence on the subtitling of cultural references. Specifically, subtitles are typically restricted to two lines on the screen, with each line containing a maximum of 37 characters. Moreover, subtitles cannot exceed a duration of six seconds. Addi- tionally, there is a requirement for precise spotting, ensuring alignment between dia- logue and subtitles. The positioning of subtitles is standardized, typically appearing at the bottom center of the screen. Finally, font selection plays a crucial role in the overall presentation of subtitles (Díaz-Cintas & Remael, 2014). As noted by Antonini (2005, p. 213), a substantial portion of utterances, ranging from 40 to 75%, undergo a reduction in lexical content. She delineates three essential procedures that subtitlers must employ to produce effective subtitles: Elimination, Rendering, and Simplification. Elimination entails the identification and removal of superfluous information within the spoken dialogue that would not be effectively conveyed through subti- tles. This process often involves eliminating repetitions, stutters, filler words such as “um,” “uh,” or “like,” as well as condensing background conversations or ambient noise descriptions. Rendering, the subsequent procedure, involves the meticulous translation of the remaining dialogue into the target language, which is typically English in this context. Finally, Simplification entails restructuring the translated subtitles to ensure clear and comprehensible presentation to the viewer (Antonini, 2005, pp. 213–214). These three procedures are intrinsically interconnected and operate in tandem to produce effective subtitles. Elimination creates the necessary space for the translator to concentrate on the most salient information. Rendering guarantees that the remaining information is accurately conveyed in the target language while considering cultural nuances. More- over, Simplification ensures that the subtitles are lucid, concise, and easily readable for the viewer. By adhering to these procedures, subtitlers can effectively bridge the 1 3 Subtitling Arabic Cultural References into English: The Case of Brando… Page 5 of 26 14 linguistic and cultural gap between the original Arabic dialogue and the English- speaking audience. Subtitling Cultural References from Arabic into English Numerous scholars within the field of translation studies have underscored the dis- tinctive challenges and intricacies inherent in the process of translating between Eng- lish and Arabic. Among these notable figures, Mona Baker and Bassam Jaber have made significant contributions to our understanding of these complexities. Baker, a prominent scholar in translation studies, has extensively explored the difficulties arising from cultural disparities, linguistic differences, and conceptual variations between the two languages. Her work, such as “In Other Words: A Coursebook on Translation,” provides valuable insights into these challenges, (Baker, 2018). Similarly, Jaber, a specialist in Arabic language and translation, has focused on the influence of sociolinguistic factors and textual analysis on the translation process, (Jaber, 2008). Their collective research has shed light on the nuanced and multifac- eted nature of English-Arabic translation, highlighting the need for a nuanced and informed approach to this complex undertaking. Studies on subtitling cultural references from Arabic into English are limited com- pared to subtitling cultural references from English into Arabic, which poses difficul- ties for researchers in this field (Thawabteh et al., 2022; Al-Adwan & Thawabteh, 2021; Ali et al., 2024). Al-Harahsheh et al. (2024) conducted a comprehensive investigation into the Translatability of Arabic Cultural References to English, focusing on the seminal novel, The Queue by Basma Abdel Aziz. The primary objective of this research was to examine the feasibility of translating cultural references embedded within Arabic literary works. Specifically, the study explored the existence of textual and matricial operational norms that are manifested in the translator’s translation processes and modifications. In their exploration of subtitling cultural references from Arabic to English, Al- Adwan and Al-Jabri (2023) presented a paper centered on the translation of metaphor- ical expressions. Their research involved analyzing how fourteen students enrolled in the Master of Arts in Audiovisual Translation program at Hamad Bin Khalifa University approached Arabic metaphors in their subtitling assignments. These stu- dents were tasked with writing commentaries on the most challenging obstacles they encountered while translating two scenes from the renowned Syrian television series Maraya. The analysis, primarily grounded in Pedersen’s (2017) translation strategies for metaphors, revealed that the students employed four distinct strategies: translat- ing a metaphor into its equivalent sense, replicating the same imagery in the tar- get language, substituting a standard target language image for the source language image, and literal translation. Conversely, Fouad (2022) conducted a descriptive study that meticulously ana- lyzed the subtitling of cultural references within five diverse Iraqi films across vari- ous genres. These cultural references were systematically categorized according to the strategies proposed by Tomaszkiewicz (1993). It is essential to note that the pri- mary objective of this research was not to evaluate the effectiveness of these subtitles 1 3 14 Page 6 of 26 A. Alquran et al. in conveying the intended meaning of the original cultural references. Rather, the focus was on investigating how cultural references were rendered in the chosen Iraqi films. A noteworthy observation is that all five films contained a total of 26 references to other cultures. The study concluded that when dealing with cultural references, subti- tlers frequently employ strategies such as literal translation, borrowing, explanation, omission, equivalency, and generalization. Among these strategies, “literal transla- tion,” “equivalency,” and “generalization” emerged as the most prevalent when the target language is English and the source language is Iraqi Arabic. This prevalence can be attributed to the existence of near-equivalent or general items in English for many Iraqi cultural references. The study further emphasized that subtitlers must possess a comprehensive under- standing of both the source and target cultures to accurately depict objects distinctive to the source culture. This understanding, coupled with the application of the previ- ously discussed methodologies, is instrumental in achieving effective subtitling of cultural references. A crucial distinction was made between Extralinguistic Cultural References (ECRs) and Interlinguistic Cultural References (ICRs). While ECRs refer to elements beyond the linguistic system of a culture, ICRs encompass idioms, proverbs, slang, and dialects, which are intrinsically linked to the culture’s linguistic framework. Through meticulous analysis, it was determined that the two most frequently used strategies in the three films were Omission and Generalization. Theoretical Framework This study adopts Pedersen’s (2005) model as its primary theoretical framework for analyzing the rendering of Extralinguistic Culture-Bound References (ECRs), here- after referred to as Cultural References (CRs). Although alternative or more recent frameworks exist, Pedersen’s model offers a systematic taxonomy for investigating how subtitlers handle cultural references that lack direct equivalents in the target lan- guage. The choice of this model is guided by its capacity to classify diverse subtitling strategies, including Retention, Specification, and Direct Translation. In addition, Pedersen’s model acknowledges the role of contextual factors such as transculturality 1 3 14 Page 8 of 26 A. Alquran et al. and the centrality of the reference, both of which are crucial when addressing cultural elements for audiences from heterogeneous backgrounds. Further, the model’s scholarly credibility and methodological reliability are rein- forced by its extensive application and empirical validation in numerous studies on subtitling and audiovisual translation (e.g., Al-Azzam et al. 2014; Sardabi & Rahimi 2020; Khoshkhoonejad & Farghadani, 2018, among others). This strong record makes the framework especially relevant to the corpus of this study, where subtitled translations form the main data. Using a framework that combines theoretical depth with proven practical value ensures not only the comparability and replicability of the findings within an existing scholarly tradition, but also that the research questions are addressed with accuracy and rigor. The present study applies Pedersen’s (2005) framework to the subtitling of CRs in the Arabic-to-English translation of the series Brando El Sharq (2023) available on the Shahid platform. Specifically, it examines the effectiveness of the strategies employed and assesses the quality of the rendered CRs through both quantitative and qualitative analyses. The study not only evaluates the applicability of Pedersen’s taxonomy to Arabic–English subtitling but also considers the emergence of strategies not explicitly outlined in Pedersen’s framework that nevertheless prove effective in rendering cultural specificity for the target audience. It is worth noting that Pedersen’s contributions to audiovisual translation have evolved over time. While his 2005 model focuses on ECRs, later iterations, par- ticularly the 2007 and 2017 refinements, expanded the scope to encompass broader cultural content. Nonetheless, the 2005 model remains the most appropriate for the present study, as the research questions are centered specifically on the subtitling of ECRs. Pedersen (2005) made a distinction between cultural references (CRs), which are extralinguistic and interlinguistic. Interlinguistic Cultural References (ICRs) are ref- erences to things only found within a culture’s linguistic system, such as idioms, proverbs, slang, and dialects; they do not refer to external reality, whereas ECRs are references to the real physical world. According to Pedersen (2005), the ECR is a “reference that is attempted by means of any culture-bound linguistic expression, which refers to an extralinguistic entity or process, and which is assumed to have a discourse referent that is identifiable to a relevant audience as this referent is within the encyclopedic knowledge of this audi- ence.” (p. 2). The model itself was developed through descriptive observations of 100 English- language films and television programs subtitled into Scandinavian languages. Draw- ing from this empirical corpus, Pedersen (2005) identified a recurrent set of subtitling strategies shaped by both linguistic norms and situational constraints. Seven strate- gies emerged from this study: Official Equivalent, Retention, Specification, Direct Translation, Generalization, Substitution, and Omission. This classification of strate- gies is utilized in the data analysis of the Brando El Shark case study. The subtitling of cultural references constitutes one of the most complex chal- lenges in audiovisual translation. It1 requires subtitlers not only to preserve semantic meaning but also to negotiate cultural nuance, audience accessibility, and medium- specific constraints such as spatial and temporal limitations. Pedersen’s (2005) taxon- 1 3 Subtitling Arabic Cultural References into English: The Case of Brando… Page 9 of 26 14 omy provides a comprehensive set of strategies through which subtitlers can mediate between source-text (ST) and target-text (TT) cultures. These strategies—ranging from strict adherence to the ST to adaptive interventions in the TT—equip subtitlers with a repertoire of techniques for resolving cultural incommensurability. The strate- gies are outlined as follows: Official Equivalent The use of an official equivalent differs from other strategies in that it is grounded in bureaucratic or institutional practice rather than in linguistic creativity. For example, the character “Donald Duck” is rendered in Swedish as Kalle Anka, a well-estab- lished equivalent that requires no further adaptation. Since the CR has already been assimilated into the TL, no translation problem arises. See Fig. 1. Retention Retention is the most closely oriented strategy toward the source language (SL). It allows an ST element to enter the TT largely unchanged, sometimes with minor orthographic or grammatical modifications to conform to TL norms. This strategy is frequently employed in rendering proper names or culturally specific designations. Retention adheres closely to the ST both in form and meaning, thereby preserving foreignness in the TT. Specification Specification involves retaining the ECR in its original form while adding details to make it more accessible to the target audience. This can occur through explicitation (e.g., spelling out acronyms such as CIA → Central Intelligence Agency) or addition (e.g., adding “city” before “Basel” to clarify the reference for Arab audiences unfa- Fig. 1 Pedersen’s taxonomy of ECR transfer strategies 1 3 14 Page 10 of 26 A. Alquran et al. miliar with the location). Through specification, subtitlers intervene directly to guide the TT audience toward correct interpretation. Direct translation Direct Translation is most applicable to institutional names, organizations, and cer- tain cultural objects. Unlike specification or generalization, it involves neither addi- tion nor reduction in semantic load. Pedersen distinguishes between Calque, which results in a literal rendering (e.g., Arabic ةيلاملا ريزو → “Minister of the Treasury”), and Shifted Direct Translation, which introduces discretionary adjustments to enhance idiomaticity (e.g., ةيبلاج → “flowing robe”). Generalization Generalization broadens the ST reference to a more generic term in the TT. For instance, “the Corinth Coffee Shop” might be translated simply as “a café.” This strategy privileges accessibility and ease of comprehension over cultural specificity, reducing potential processing difficulties for the TT audience. Substitution Substitution replaces an unfamiliar ECR with a culturally accessible equivalent in the TT. Pedersen identifies two subtypes: ● Cultural substitution, in which a culturally bound item is replaced with a compa- rable, familiar item in the TL (e.g., the UK Home Office rendered into Arabic as ةيلخادلا ةرازو [Ministry of Interior]). ● Paraphrasing, which rewords the ECR either by transferring its sense (e.g., ىولح يلع مأ (Umm Ali seewts)→ “bread pudding with nuts and raisins”) or by situation- ally rephrasing the expression (e.g., كعم الله [“Allah be with you”] → “goodbye”). Omission Omission entails leaving the ECR untranslated, effectively removing it from the TT. This strategy is often employed when retaining the reference would obstruct com- prehension, exceed subtitle space, or provide culturally irrelevant information. For example, references to culturally specific military traditions, such as the Qatari Bar- zan Towers as a symbol of defense, may be omitted in subtitled war films if they do not contribute to narrative progression. While omission can streamline readability, it risks erasing cultural nuance and reducing textual authenticity. For this reason, omission is generally considered a last resort to be applied sparingly and with careful justification. 1 3 Subtitling Arabic Cultural References into English: The Case of Brando… Page 11 of 26 14 Case Study and Methodology Case Study Brando El Sharq (meaning “Brando of the East”) is a 2023 Lebanese Arabic-lan- guage dialect black comedy series released on the Shahid platform, a subscription- based video-on-demand service offered by the MBC Group. Brando El Sharq falls under the black com- edy genre, known for its dark humor and satirical elements. It explores the often- challenging realities faced by filmmakers, particularly within the independent film scene. The series is directed by Amin Dora and produced by Sadek Sabbah from Cedar Arts Productions. The core cast features established actors in the Arab world, including Amal Arafa, Jihad Saad, Camille Salameh, Zeina Makki, and Talal Jurdi. The presence of these actors might suggest that the series aims to attract a broad Arab audience familiar with these prominent figures. The series Brando El Sharq was chosen for analysis based on several key criteria. First, its contemporary context as a 2023 production ensures that its cultural ref- erences accurately reflect modern Arab society. This makes it particularly relevant for examining how these references are handled in subtitling for English-speaking audiences. Second, its genre as a black comedy adds another layer of complexity, as it often employs culturally specific humor and social critique. This provides an opportunity to explore how such elements are adapted for an English-speaking audi- ence, especially through subtitling. Additionally, the series’ focus on the film industry introduces references to Arab filmmaking practices, jargon, and comedic techniques unique to the Arab world. Analyzing how these elements are subtitled can reveal valuable insights into the challenges and strategies associated with translating cul- turally rich content. Furthermore, its release on Shahid, a major Arabic streaming platform with international reach, suggests that the show is likely subtitled for Eng- lish-speaking viewers, enabling a direct comparison between the original Arabic and the English subtitles. Finally, the directionality of translation from Arabic to English is a critical aspect of this analysis, as it involves addressing cultural nuances, idioms, wordplay, humor, and satire that may not have direct equivalents in English. Methodology This research is a descriptive and evaluative study as it aims to identify whether the utilized model succeeded in conveying the original meaning of the CRs of the ST to the TT and to locate the mistranslations, if any. This research takes a qualitative approach to analyze subtitles for Brando El Sharq series on “Shahid.” The goals are to identify the most frequently used strategies employed in translating the dialogue of the series into subtitles, assess the accuracy of the subtitles in conveying the orig- inal meaning, and identify any particularly successful strategies. These successful strategies could then be incorporated into the subtitling model proposed by Pedersen (2005). 1 3 14 Page 12 of 26 A. Alquran et al. To do so, I started by carefully examining each example to identify the specific cultural reference embedded within the Arabic text in the ten episodes of Brando El Sharq (2023). This included understanding the literal meaning of the words and phrases, as well as any cultural connotations or significance they might hold. Next, I analyzed how the cultural reference was translated into English. This involved look- ing for the specific subtitling technique used, such as Official Equivalent, Calque Direct Translation, Shifted Direct Translation, Paraphrase with Sense Transfer, or another strategy. I then evaluated how effectively the subtitling strategy conveyed the meaning of the cultural reference for an English audience. This considered whether the subtitling accurately captured the original concept, including any cultural nuances or implications. Finally, I assessed the clarity and flow of the translated text. This ensured that the subtitling strategy maintained a natural-sounding English sentence structure while effectively integrating the cultural reference. Then, I categorized my examples according to the taxonomy of the strategies. To this end, I used a table that includes the number of examples, the original Arabic subtitle, the English subtitle, and the strategy’s name. The literal and implied meaning of the sentence is ‘Do not buy fish from the sea before catching it.’ Therefore, the subtitler chose to avoid a literal translation that might distort the overall meaning. Instead, s/he opted for situational paraphrasing, giving full consideration to the context and rendering it in a way that fits the situa- tion while avoiding a direct literal translation. Another strategy that could have been employed is cultural substitution, but the subtitler decided not to recruit it, as it would require more space and time, thereby violating the established norms and guidelines of subtitling. Cultural Substitution Cultural substitution emerged as the second most prevalent strategy employed by the subtitler. While the Direct Translation strategy was utilized on 110 occasions, repre- senting a frequency of 21%, cultural substitution was implemented more frequently. In this strategy, the subtitler replaces the cultural reference with one that resonates with the target culture, conveying analogous connotations. The following examples illustrate how the subtitler effectively applied cultural substitution in this study. Below are two illustrative examples: Example 3 (episode no. 7; time: 18:42): Source text Target text ءاوه لكُ Shut up! Back translation: Eat air. Context Karim gives his friend Youssef advice on how to get closer to Lama, but Youssef doesn’t like one of the pieces of advice, so he tells Karim to shut up. In this example, the phrase كل الهواء, meaning ‘eat air’, is not a commonly under- stood offensive expression. Had the subtitler translated it as ‘eat dust,’ it would have changed the overall meaning. Therefore, they opted for culturally substituting it with 1 3 Subtitling Arabic Cultural References into English: The Case of Brando… Page 15 of 26 14 ‘shut up!’, thus effectively conveying not only the intended meaning but also the language user’s negative attitude. Example 4 (episode no. 8; time: 23:35): Source text Target text .هلحم كلاح يطح Put yourself in his shoes Back translation: Put yourself in his place Context Ghassan talks to Salwa and defends Youssef because he is very busy coordi- nating the completion of the film, so he tells her to put yourself in his place. Here, although the literal translation would have been understandable to the target audience, the subtitler opted for a cultural substitution with a more idiomatic expres- sion, ensuring that the overall meaning was preserved and the established norms and guidelines of subtitling were not violated. Direct Translation Direct translation emerged as the third most frequently employed strategy by the sub- titler, with a frequency of 14%. This approach was utilized on 70 occasions. Certain names of historical or mythical significance may inadvertently convey misleading connotations, potentially exerting a negative impact when the retention strategy is applied. So, he says to Youssef: ‘’You spent years writing your own Trojan horse’’. The subtitler, as one may observe, decided not to attempt to find a cultural equiva- lent for the Trojan Horse. Instead, s/he opted to use the direct translation technique, relying on the structure and vocabulary used to unravel the intended meaning. Example 6 (episode no. 1; time: 15:32): Source text Target text ؟كعبت سورعلا ةمرب انلتلمع مويلا نامك ؟وش What? Did you do your rounds today like a bride? Back translation: What? The translator, as can be seen, opted for a direct trans- lation, likely because the target culture lacks such a concept, which may leave the audience confused and necessitate extra effort to grasp the intended meaning. Omission Omission emerged as the fourth most frequently employed strategy by the subtitler, with a frequency of 6%. This approach was utilized on 30 occasions within the target text. Omission is particularly effective in addressing forms of profanity and swear words. Omission can be employed for several reasons. In examples 7 and 8, the sub- titler, as can be observed, chose to omit content deemed potentially offensive. Context Youssef was surprised by the arrival of a friend of his neighbor, whom he admired. When he saw him hugging her, he said: Where did he come from? In examples 9 and 10, however, the subtitler, after having considered the tar- get audience’s lack of familiarity with certain Islamic concepts, resorted to omit- ting these Islamic expressions. Translating them literally, the subtitler might have thought, would likely strike the target language readers as unusual, thereby hindering effective communication. 1 3 Subtitling Arabic Cultural References into English: The Case of Brando… Page 17 of 26 14 Example 9 (episode no. 4; time: 07:31): Source text Target text هقزري الله سب - Back translation: But God may provide him with what he needs. Retention Retention emerged as the fifth most used strategy by subtitlers. In the context of sub- titling cultural references (CRs) from Arabic dialects (such as Lebanese Arabic) into English, retention refers to the practice of preserving the original Arabic term in the subtitles. This strategy prioritizes fidelity to the ST, assuming that the target audience has some prior knowledge or can infer meaning from contextual cues. Retention is particularly suited to CRs that lack direct English equivalents or for cases where a literal translation might be inadequate or imprecise. Additionally, it is often used for references that carry significant cultural weight or meaning in the Arabic source text. It is worth highlighting that certain renowned streaming platforms, such as Netflix, have adopted a retention strategy in their subtitling guidelines for English-to-Arabic translations. This strategy is particularly applied to proper names, singers, actors, music bands, and place names with global recognition. These guidelines require sub- titlers to maintain fidelity to the original language by transliterating proper names in the content. This applies even to Arabic versions of names such as Isaac, Jesus, Jacob, Abraham, Luka, and others. ‘Jasmin’, for instance, should be retained as نيمساج, not نيمساي (netflixstudios 2024). Data analysis shows that the subtitler opted for the retention strategy in handling most proper names, such as Tannous Afif Al-Jouri, Youssef Tamer, Sabine Rahim, to mention but some. Although this strategy demonstrated fidelity to the original text, thus preserving the essence of the source culture, it fails to evoke the same connota- tions in the minds of the target language readers, as shown in this example: 1 3 14 Page 18 of 26 A. Alquran et al. Example 11 (episode no. 1; time: 52): Source text Target text .هتيزمر ولإ ،امس ؟مسلاا ولح شم Isn’t it a beautiful name? The name Sama has symbols. Back translation: Isn’t it a beautiful name? Sama has symbols. Context In the introduction to the series, Youssef was telling the story of the film he would produce and mentioned the name of the film’s star, Sama, and the symbolism of her name. In this example, سما, used in Arabic, is a feminine name derived from the verb ‘to ascend,’ carrying connotations of height, elevation, and status. Therefore, opting for the retention strategy in this context would not evoke the same connotations in the minds of the target language readers, thus missing the symbolic and semantic nuances associated with the name in Arabic. Generalization Generalization emerged as the sixth most frequently employed strategy by the subti- tler, with a frequency of 2.5%. This strategy was utilized on 13 occasions. I had no money on me Back translation: Shut up. He offered to pay for the benzene, and I did not have any lira Context Youssef praises Samih for paying for the gas since he didn’t have any lira. In this example, as one may notice, the word نيزنب, i.e. gasoline, was rendered as ‘fuel,’ and the word ةريل, i.e. lira, was translated as ‘money.’ In translating these words, the subtitler opted for generalization. The established equivalents of نيزنب and ةريل, meaning ‘gasoline’ and ‘lira,’ respectively, are generally understood by most English speakers in the context of vehicles and currency; however, the subtitler likely opted for generalization to ensure readability, acceptability, and accessibility that would feed into naturalness (Almanna & House, 2023: 122). 1 3 Subtitling Arabic Cultural References into English: The Case of Brando… Page 19 of 26 14 Example 13 (episode no. 9; time: 16:51): Source text Target text كنم ةملك ىنتسيب دحاو ةيم A lot of men would do anything to please you Back translation: One hundred are waiting for a word from you. Being fully aware of this nuanced meaning, the subtitler opted to add the noun phrase ‘the world’ to convey the intended meaning accurately. Findings and Discussion Subtitling and analyzing Brando El Sharq proved to be a formidable challenge due to its rich tapestry of cultural references and the hybrid nature of its dialogue, which incorporates Arabic, English, and French vocabulary. Translating a single cultural reference from Arabic to English often necessitated a combination of two or three strategies from Pedersen’s (2005) model, as cultural references are deeply embedded within the source language and culture, carrying nuanced meanings and associations that may lack direct equivalents in the target language. Moreover, a single word or phrase in Arabic can encapsulate a rich layer of meaning, contingent upon contextual understanding. Consequently, capturing this nuance in English can be a demanding task. Data analysis indicates that the subtitlers of the Brando El Sharq (2023) series have systematically employed all the strategies identified in Pedersen’s (2005) taxon- 1 3 Subtitling Arabic Cultural References into English: The Case of Brando… Page 21 of 26 14 omy. Among these, paraphrasing, cultural substitution, direct translation, and omis- sion stood out as the most commonly adopted techniques. Although these strategies have undoubtedly enhanced the text’s accessibility for the intended audience, they have occasionally introduced discrepancies in expressive meaning due to the subtitler’s choice of less-than-ideal cultural equivalents. Retention, to elaborate, proved to be a practical approach for rendering proper names. However, it inadvertently led to a loss of expressive meaning and connota- tion. Consequently, the symbolism associated with names was compromised in sev- eral instances where retention was employed. Although retention was effective in certain scenarios, it often resulted in the erosion of connotative meaning in numerous utterances. As observed in the corpus, the analysis of selected subtitle translations tentatively suggests that Brando El Sharq may have been produced by multiple subtitlers rather than a single practitioner. The proper noun ‘Youssef’, for example, was rendered in three distinct orthographic forms: Youssef, Youcef, and Yusuf, which could indicate transliteration inconsistency across the data set. Similarly, the series title was, on one occasion, rendered as ‘Brando of the East’ instead of ‘Brando El Sharq’, a deviation that may further point to limited standardization in the subtitling process. To verify this matter, a series of email correspondences was initiated with the rel- evant parties. However, despite our repeated attempts and follow-ups, the responses received did not yield any further information. Added to this, the subtitler(s), in some instances, failed to convey the original meaning. The following section presents some illustrative examples to explain this point. Inaccurate Subtitling In these instances, as well as in several others, the subtitler(s) were unable to fully convey the original meaning of the text. Despite efforts to maintain accuracy, certain nuances and cultural references seem to have been lost or misrepresented, thus lead- ing to a divergence from the intended message. Example 17 (episode no. 6; time: 08:39): Source text Target text ؟يّيب نيو يتلاخ Where is my aunt, dad? Back translation: My aunt, where is my dad? Context Youssef, confused, asked his father incorrectly: Aunt, where is my father? Here, as one may observe, Youssef was asking his aunt about his dad. However, the subtitler inverted the roles, presenting the conversation in a way that fundamen- tally alters the intended meaning. 1 3 14 Page 22 of 26 A. Alquran et al. Example 18 (episode no. 3; time: 07:23): Source text Target text كيف تيلخات مربا مع تقو يل راص Time is passing quickly? Back translation: I’ve spent so much time looking for you just to be able to talk to you alone. Context Jenny follows Youssef in her car and finds him after his friends have pranked him. She urges him to come with her, and once he agrees, she expresses her relief at finally being able to have a private conversation. Here, as can be seen, the subtitler failed to figure out the intended meaning, thereby translating it inaccurately as ‘Time is passing quickly’. Context After Jenney told Youssef that she had spent a lot of time looking for him just to be able to talk to him alone, he felt guilty, thus saying: “Shame on me”. In this example, the subtitler failed again to understand the meaning of موشلا بيع اي, a phrase used by people in informal conversations to express the embarrassment and discomfort they feel as a result of their own unintentional behavior, particularly when they were expected to be more attentive. Opting for ‘Thank you’ not only changes the intended meaning but also negatively affects the coherence of the text. Example 20 (episode no. 4; time: 25:01): Source text Target text دهشملا يوق ،يوق Brave, brave seen Back translation: Context In front of Youssef, Samih praises the scene he will act out and says: “Brave scene”. Here, as one may notice, the subtitler made a spelling error with the word ‘scene’, which resulted in a notable distortion of the intended meaning. This seemingly small mistake has the potential to confuse the viewer, altering the context and undermining the accuracy of the translation. 1 3 Subtitling Arabic Cultural References into English: The Case of Brando… Page 23 of 26 14 The subtitler’s failure to accurately render cultural references can be attributed to several factors. Tight deadlines and limited resources can significantly impede the quality of subtitling. Moreover, a lack of familiarity with the source text can hinder the subtitler’s ability to conduct thorough research or explore alternative translation strategies for cultural references. The pressure of these deadlines may compel subti- tlers to opt for direct translations, which can lead to confusion or inaccuracies when cultural references lack direct equivalents in the target language. A lack of under- standing of the source culture and its specific references can result in misinterpreta- tions of jokes, proverbs, historical allusions, and other cultural elements within the text. Further, space and time constraints may pose challenges in providing compre- hensive explanations for complex cultural references. Despite the aforementioned shortcomings, including instances of mistranslation and the use of unsuitable strategies, the subtitlers were successful, to a significant extent, in bridging the cultural gap between Arabic and English. To improve the qual- ity of future subtitles, it is essential for subtitlers to act as insiders in the source cul- ture, thus being able to comprehend the specific cultural references embedded within the original text. Failing to act as insiders for any reason, they need to adopt an outsider perspective, seeking advice from experts or native speakers fluent in the source culture. This can provide invaluable insights, thus ensuring greater accuracy and cultural sensitivity. Moreover, subtitlers need to focus on refining their approach to cultural references by carefully selecting the most effective strategies and considering the use of innovative techniques such as footnotes, annotations, or slightly extended subtitles. By adopt- ing these measures, subtitlers can greatly enhance the viewing experience, making it more accessible and meaningful for audiences from diverse cultural backgrounds. Study Limitations The study is subject to several limitations that constrain the scope and transferability of its findings. First, its focus on a single television series, Brando El Sharq (2023), in the Lebanese Arabic dialect over ten episodes narrows the generalizability of results across dialects, genres (e.g., drama, comedy, action), and audiovisual formats (film, series, documentary), with cultural references that are often specific to Lebanese society and therefore not representative of broader Arabic-speaking contexts. Sec- ond, the reliance on dialectal material introduces challenges, since certain cultural references are highly localized, tied to slang or idioms, and potentially opaque even to other Arabic speakers; the subtitler’s comprehension of such dialectal nuances plays a critical role, yet the processes behind these choices remain inaccessible for analysis. The focus on Brando El Sharq (2023), while limited in scope, provides an in-depth case study that highlights the complex subtitling of Lebanese Arabic cultural references, an area rarely investigated in comparison to more frequently studied vari- eties such as Egyptian or Modern Standard Arabic. Finally, the research design is descriptive and non-experimental, focusing on textual analysis of subtitles without testing alternative renderings or engaging in audience-based evaluation. However, the study systematically documents transla- tion strategies and missteps in a way that enhances our understanding of subtitling 1 3 14 Page 24 of 26 A. Alquran et al. practices in Arabic–English contexts. The absence of audience reception data, while narrowing the scope of conclusions, also highlights a clear path for further empirical research into how viewers actually perceive subtitled cultural references. Conclusion This study has illustrated the intricacy of translating Arabic cultural references into English subtitles using the case of Brando El Sharq. Utilizing Pedersen’s (2005) tax- onomy, the investigation elucidated both the adaptability and constraints of current subtitling methodologies, emphasizing that paraphrase, cultural substitution, and direct translation were predominantly employed to reconcile language and cultural disparities. However, the findings also reveal the difficulties involved in conveying meaning when cultural subtleties hinder direct translation, especially in instances where connotative richness or symbolic significance is diminished. The analysis revealed significant variance and inconsistency in the treatment of these cultural references, corroborating the initial premise that the English subtitles were probably created by multiple translators. The observed transitions in methodol- ogy, from source-focused methods such as retention to target-focused strategies like generalization, indicate the absence of a cohesive subtitling policy or style guide for the series. The results emphasize the need to view subtitling not solely as a technical task of linguistic conversion but as a cultural negotiation influenced by audience expec- tations, platform norms, and the translator’s interpretive authority. Practically, this necessitates that subtitlers operating between Arabic and English must reconcile faithfulness to the original culture with accessibility for international audiences, an endeavor that demands both linguistic proficiency and cultural insider insight. Theo- retically, the study substantiates Pedersen’s model as a significant analytical instru- ment, while simultaneously indicating the necessity for its enhancement to address hybrid tactics and emerging issues in the field of audiovisual translation. This research not only details subtitling choices but also elucidates the intricate issues of rendering culturally rich information accessible to a worldwide audience. The discrepancies in the subtitles illustrate the fundamental conflict between main- taining cultural authenticity and facilitating audience understanding. While several decisions successfully spanned the cultural divide, others unintentionally diminished cultural distinctiveness or created opportunities for misinterpretation. The results emphasize that subtitling transcends a simple linguistic function and constitutes a cultural negotiation. The findings of this study offer valuable insights for subtitlers working with Arabic-to-English cultural references, providing a framework for selecting the most appropriate strategies. Furthermore, this research has identified several mistransla- tions and unsuitable strategies that appeared within the series, suggesting potential corrections and alternative approaches for effectively conveying cultural references. Future research could delve into the audience’s perspective on the effectiveness of various subtitling strategies in understanding cultural references. Investigating viewers’ preferences and comprehension levels across diverse cultural backgrounds 1 3 Subtitling Arabic Cultural References into English: The Case of Brando… Page 25 of 26 14 would be particularly valuable. Additionally, exploring the subtitling of other cultural phenomena, such as humour, politeness markers, and profanity, could offer more profound insights. JSON: Name: arabic_cr_subtitling_pedersen Title: A corpus-based evaluation of Pedersen-informed subtitling strategies for translating Lebanese Arabic cultural references into English Short Hypothesis: Subtitling cultural references from Lebanese Arabic into English using Pedersen-informed strategies emphasizing situational paraphrase and cultural substitution causes higher target-audience comprehension accuracy than subtitling using direct translation or retention. Related Work: Prior work establishes a small set of empirical taxonomies and descriptive frameworks for handling extralinguistic cultural references in audiovisual translation, most prominently Pedersen's seven-strategy taxonomy, as well as ad hoc lists of strategies (literal translation, borrowing, explanation, omission, equivalency, generalization). Existing studies have applied these taxonomies qualitatively to isolated films/episodes or student exercises and have reported frequent use of paraphrase, substitution, omission and retention. Limitations across current approaches include reliance on small, non-representative samples, lack of controlled viewer comprehension testing, inconsistent operational definitions across studies, limited treatment of dialectal variation, lack of inter-annotator reliability reporting, and sparse quantitative comparisons between strategy types or between human and automatic methods. There is also little work evaluating how strategy choice affects narrative comprehension, perceived naturalness, or cross-cultural connotation preservation. Abstract: This project addresses the problem of how subtitling choices affect English-speaking viewers' comprehension of cultural references (CRs) originating in Lebanese Arabic. We propose a structured research pipeline that (1) constructs a validated corpus of CR tokens and aligned English subtitle variants; (2) annotates each CR with applied strategy labels using Pedersen's taxonomy plus documented extensions; and (3) evaluates the impact of specific strategy classes on human comprehension, perceived naturalness, and semantic adequacy. The main contribution is an empirically grounded mapping from subtitling strategy to measurable viewer outcomes and an annotated corpus for reproducible research. Expected outcomes include quantified differences in comprehension and naturalness across strategy classes, robust inter-annotator agreement statistics, and a ranked set of strategies optimized for comprehension by English viewers of Lebanese-Arabic content. The resulting dataset and analyses will enable evidence-based subtitling guidelines and provide a benchmark for automated strategy-selection tools. Experiments: Datasets: (A) Primary corpus: annotated subtitle corpus of Brando El Sharq (10 episodes, ~502 CR instances) including source utterance, context clip, original English subtitle, and human-proposed alternate subtitles per strategy; (B) Validation corpus: two additional Lebanese Arabic audiovisual works (combined ~300 CR instances) for generalization testing; (C) Synthetic controlled stimuli: 120 short clips (6–12s) created to isolate individual CR types. Annotation: two trained annotators label strategy applied (Pedersen categories + 'transcreation' and 'hybrid') and provide confidence; compute Cohen's kappa. Baselines: original platform subtitles; direct-translation baseline (literal rendering); retention baseline (transliteration); machine-translated baseline (state-of-the-art MT post-edited to subtitle length); Pedersen-informed human rewrites (paraphrase, substitution, specification). Evaluation metrics: comprehension accuracy (percent correct on 3–4 multiple-choice content+CR questions per clip), semantic adequacy and fluency (5-point Likert by blinded native English raters), perceived naturalness (5-point Likert), reading load (characters-per-second and reading ease), inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa), correlation between automatic metrics (BLEU, METEOR, chrF) and human adequacy. Experimental setup: within-subjects randomized blocks where each participant (n=120 English-only viewers; n=40 bilingual Arabic-English viewers) watches a balanced subset of clips with different subtitle variants; counterbalance order; collect response time and accuracy. Analysis: pairwise comparisons (paired t-tests / Wilcoxon) between strategy groups for comprehension and naturalness; ANOVA for multi-group effects; effect size reporting (Cohen's d). Ablation: remove specification and paraphrase from Pedersen-informed set to measure drop in comprehension; evaluate classifier ablation where automatic strategy-prediction model is trained on full features vs. without context embeddings. Generalization test: apply top-performing strategies to validation corpus and report transfer of effect sizes. Risk Factors and Limitations: Annotation variability and low inter-annotator agreement due to ambiguous CR boundaries and mixed dialectal forms; limited generalizability because dataset focuses on one series and Lebanese dialect, which may not represent other Arabic varieties; participant sampling bias (online volunteers may not match target platform demographics); ecological validity: short experimental clips may not replicate narrative engagement of full-episode viewing; automatic metrics (BLEU/METEOR) may correlate poorly with human comprehension and adequacy; strategy interactions: multi-strategy or hybrid renderings complicate causal attribution of effects; resource constraints: acquiring subtitle files and licensing clips for experiments may be restricted; compute limits for training strategy-prediction models on small annotated datasets may lead to overfitting; subtitle timing and screen-space constraints are not fully modeled in textual variants, limiting realism of some tested renditions.
